answer: Net billing in Pakistan charges every imported unit at your normal slab rate and credits each exported unit at a flat buyback rate, reported at about {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} but not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page. Net bill = imports × slab rate − exports × buyback rate: importing {{in.import_units|int}} and exporting {{in.export_units|int}} units costs {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}, against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} under old net metering.
how: Import: {{out.import_units}} units × {{out.import_rate|rs2}} = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}. Export credit: {{out.export_units}} units × {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} = {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}. Net billing energy charge = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} − {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} = {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} (credit carried forward: {{out.carry_forward_rs|rs}}). Old net metering: {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units × {{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Net billing costs {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. Fixed charges, surcharges, adjustments and GST come on top of both.
key_facts: Pakistan replaced net metering with net billing for new solar connections under the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}: imported units are billed at the normal slab rate and exported units are credited at a separate buyback rate.

The net billing buyback rate was not confirmed on a NEPRA page when Wattlyst last checked ({{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_checked}}); news reports put it at about {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit, far below the {{out.import_rate|rs2}} slab rate of a {{out.import_units|int}} unit month.

For a month with {{out.import_units|int}} units imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported, net billing charges {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} in energy against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} under old net metering, {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more.
Under net billing the solar system you may connect is reported to be capped at your sanctioned load, so the sanctioned load on the bill sets the largest system you can apply for.
Whether existing net-metering contracts keep the old one-for-one rules until they expire is widely reported but not confirmed on a NEPRA page; ask your DISCO which regime your connection is on.

formula.text: Net billing Rs = max(0, imported units × slab rate − exported units × buyback rate); old net metering Rs = max(0, imported − exported) × slab rate of the net units
lines: slab rate = A-1 domestic rate of the band the imported units reach (unprotected or protected)
buyback rate = flat Rs per exported unit; editable because it is not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page
a credit larger than the import bill carries forward in rupees; the bill is never negative
energy charges only: fixed charge, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST are added on the real bill

p: Until 2026 a home solar system in Pakistan was connected under net metering: a bidirectional meter counted units in and units out, and the DISCO billed only the difference. The {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, moved new connections to net billing. The meter is the same kind, but the two readings are now priced separately: imports at the normal tariff, exports at a buyback rate.

The change matters because the two prices are far apart. Under net metering an exported unit was worth as much as an imported one; under net billing it is worth the buyback rate, a fraction of the slab rate. Using your own solar power during the day is now worth much more than sending it to the grid.

sections.h2: Net billing vs net metering in Pakistan: a worked month
p: Take a month with {{out.import_units|int}} units imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported. Net metering would bill {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units at {{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}}, which is {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Net billing bills all {{out.import_units|int}} imported units at {{out.import_rate|rs2}} ({{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}) and credits {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} for the exports, leaving {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}.

The gap comes from two places: the low buyback rate, and the slab. Under net metering the net units could fall into a cheaper band; under net billing the imported units alone set the band. A home that exports more than it imports still pays something under net billing, as the second example below shows.

sections.h2: NEPRA net billing buyback rate: what is confirmed
p: Not the rate itself. When Wattlyst last checked ({{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_checked}}) there was no NEPRA notification of the buyback rate; news reports put it at about {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit, with one report giving a lower figure; two of the reports are listed under Sources. The calculator uses the reported figure as a default and lets you change it.

The rate is expected to follow the national average power purchase price and to be revised over time. When your DISCO or NEPRA publishes it, enter it in the buyback field; the table below shows how much the monthly bill moves for each rupee of buyback.

sections.h2: Sanctioned load cap: how big can a net billing system be?
p: Under the new rules the solar system you may connect is reported to be capped at your sanctioned load: the kW printed as sanctioned load on your bill is the largest solar system you could connect. If you want a larger system you have to apply for a higher sanctioned load first, which raises the fixed charge every month and, at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more, moves the connection to a time-of-use meter.
Size the connection with the sanctioned load calculator before you size the panels, and check the cap with your DISCO, since the regulation text was not available to us on the NEPRA site.

sections.h2: Is net metering ending in Pakistan? Existing contracts
p: For new applications, yes: they are processed under net billing. For homes already on net metering, news reports say the existing agreements stay on the old one-for-one terms until they expire, after which renewal would be on net billing. This is not confirmed on a NEPRA page, so treat it as likely rather than certain and ask your DISCO what applies to your agreement and when it ends.

sections.h2: Net metering application: the steps in general
p: The steps are broadly the same under net billing as they were under net metering, but the forms and documents differ between DISCOs, so confirm each step with yours. First, check the sanctioned load on your bill and size the system within it. Second, choose an installer your DISCO accepts; under the net-metering rules this meant a vendor registered with the Alternative Energy Development Board.

Third, the installer or you submit the application to the DISCO with the system details, the latest bill and identity documents. Fourth, the DISCO checks the connection and approves it, and an agreement is signed. Fifth, the DISCO installs the bidirectional meter and the system starts exporting. Do not switch on export before the meter is installed.

sections.h2: What net billing means for solar payback
p: Payback now depends mostly on how much of the solar output you use yourself. Every unit used at home saves the full slab rate of {{out.import_rate|rs2}}; every unit exported earns the buyback rate. Run the pump, washing machine, iron and AC in the day, and size the system to your daytime use rather than to the roof.
To estimate payback, take the system price from the solar price pages and divide it by the yearly saving: the bill you would pay without solar minus the net billing bill, over twelve months.

mistakes: Taking the reported buyback rate as final. It is not confirmed on a NEPRA page; use the rate printed on your own bill or DISCO notice.
Assuming an existing net-metering agreement is safe forever. Reports say it continues until it expires, but this is unconfirmed; check the end date with your DISCO.
Sizing the system to the roof instead of to the sanctioned load and daytime use. Under net billing the system is reported to be capped at the sanctioned load, and exported units earn little.
Reading the result as the full bill. It is the energy charge only; fixed charges, surcharges, adjustments and GST are added on the real bill.
safety: Only a DISCO-approved installer and a licensed electrician may connect a solar system for export, and only the DISCO installs the bidirectional meter; never back-feed the grid through a socket or bypass the meter.

faq.q: What is net billing in Pakistan?
faq.a: A way of billing solar homes in which imported units are charged at the normal slab rate and exported units are credited at a lower buyback rate, about {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit in news reports. It replaced net metering for new connections under the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between net billing and net metering?
faq.a: Net metering subtracted exported units from imported units and billed the difference. Net billing prices them separately: imports at the slab rate, exports at the buyback rate. For {{out.import_units|int}} units in and {{out.export_units|int}} out that is {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}.

faq.q: What is the NEPRA net billing buyback rate?
faq.a: Not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page when we last checked ({{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_checked}}). News reports give about {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit. Enter the rate on your bill in the calculator.

faq.q: Is net metering ending in Pakistan?
faq.a: For new connections, yes: they get net billing. Existing net-metering agreements are reported to continue until they expire, but this is not confirmed on a NEPRA page; ask your DISCO.

faq.q: How big a solar system can I connect under net billing?
faq.a: Reports on the new rules say up to your sanctioned load, so the sanctioned kW on your bill is the largest system you could connect. A higher sanctioned load raises the fixed charge and, at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more, means a time-of-use meter.

faq.q: How do I apply for net billing?
faq.a: Through your DISCO, usually via the installer: size the system within your sanctioned load, apply with the system details, latest bill and identity documents, wait for the DISCO's approval and agreement, then the DISCO fits a bidirectional meter. Documents vary by DISCO.

faq.q: Is solar still worth it under net billing?
faq.a: Usually yes, if most of the output is used at home in the day: each self-used unit saves the full slab rate of {{out.import_rate|rs2}}, while an exported unit earns only the buyback rate. Size the system to daytime use.
